name: Sunless tan / body makeup to hide marks

card.summary: Self-tanner and body makeup that visually blend stretch marks and scars; the effect is temporary and cosmetic.
card.aka: Self-tanner, DHA tan, bronzer, body foundation, camouflage makeup
card.note: Color fades in days and gives no UV protection; DHA is not approved for inhalation or use around eyes and lips.

quick.overview:
Sunless tanners and body makeup are used to reduce the contrast between marks such as stretch marks or scars and the surrounding skin. Tanners darken the surface skin chemically, while bronzers and makeup add temporary color that washes off.[1][2]

The effects last from hours (makeup, bronzer) to roughly a week (DHA tanners), and no controlled studies of these products specifically for hiding stretch marks or scars were found.
quick.mechanism: DHA (dihydroxyacetone), typically 3 to 5 percent in products, reacts with amino acids in the dead outer layer of skin to produce a brown color that fades over about 3 to 10 days. Bronzers and camouflage makeup are pigments that sit on the skin and wash off.[1][2]
quick.risks: A tan from DHA does not protect against UV, and sunscreen added to tanners wears off quickly.[1] The FDA has approved DHA for external use but not for the eyes, lips, mucous membranes or inhalation; contact dermatitis has been reported, and laboratory studies have reported DNA damage and free-radical formation, though a 2010 EU scientific committee opinion found spray tanning posed no risk.[1]

lead: Sunless tanning and body makeup are cosmetic ways to even out skin tone and visually mask marks such as stretch marks (striae) and scars without a procedure. People use them to look more bronzed and to reduce the contrast between a mark and the surrounding skin. Sunless tanners darken the skin with a reactive ingredient, usually dihydroxyacetone (DHA), while bronzers and camouflage makeup apply removable pigment.[1][2]

Wikipedia's article on cosmetic camouflage lists acne, scars, stretch marks, vitiligo, tattoos and bruises among conditions such creams conceal, and says camouflage may reduce the psychological impact of skin imperfections.[2] On looksmax.org, members discuss self-tanners for the face and body, bronzer and contour for changing facial appearance, and bronzer for darker complexions.[7][8][9][10]

Research on these products has focused on tan colour and on who uses them rather than on masking marks. A 2000 study compared the tone of DHA tans with sun tans,[5] and a 2018 national survey analysis found 6.4% of US adults reported sunless tanning.[4] No published trial has tested sunless tanner specifically for hiding stretch marks or scars.
infobox: DHA approved by FDA for external use only

paras: Sunless tanning products fall into two groups: skin-reactive agents, mainly DHA (sometimes with erythrulose, which develops more slowly), and temporary bronzers that wash off with soap and water.[1] Products come as lotions, gradual-tanning moisturisers, mousses, sprays, and salon airbrush or booth applications.[1]

Camouflage makeup is a related category of creams and powders intended to hide color or texture irregularities on the face or body. The Wikipedia article on cosmetic camouflage says such creams were first developed by plastic surgeons during World War II to cover burns, and that green concealer is commonly suggested to neutralise redness.[2]

DHA is not a dye or paint; it reacts with amino acids in the dead outer skin layer, and its concentration determines how dark the result is. The color fades gradually as skin cells shed, over about 3 to 10 days.[1]

Applied over a scar or stretch mark, tanner and makeup aim to reduce contrast with surrounding skin. Because striae are scars of the dermis and often differ in texture as well as color, texture is not changed by these products.[3]

Eva Wittgenstein noticed DHA staining skin in the 1950s. Man-Tan (1959) and Coppertone's QT (1960) were the first commercial DHA self-tanners, and their orange tones gave the category a poor reputation until later reformulations and, from the late 1990s, automated spray booths broadened the market.[1]

A 2000 study measured the colour of sun tans in volunteers and compared it with DHA tans on standard chroma and red/yellow charts. Its authors noted that DHA colour is similar to a suntan but can be somewhat more yellow, and they tested ways to improve the tonality of sunless tans.[5]

A 2010 laboratory and volunteer study of two DHA formulations that differed only in their rheology modifier found differences in colour development, showing that the base formula, as well as DHA concentration, affects the resulting shade.[6]

Looksmax.org members post about self-tanner for the face, rankings of tanners, and corrections when application goes patchy. In one thread a user who missed spots around the eyes, mouth and hairline asked how to fix uneven orange colour; a reply suggested abrasive scrubbing to remove it.[7] Other thread titles discuss bronzer for darker complexions and using bronzer and contour to reshape the look of the face.[8][9][10]

The FDA approved DHA for external use but not around the eyes, on lips, on mucous membranes or for inhalation, and has noted that all-over spray booth application can make such exposures hard to avoid.[1] DHA and erythrulose can cause contact dermatitis, and fragrances, preservatives and other ingredients in tanners are also potential allergens.[1]

A 2007 study found skin treated with DHA formed more free radicals under sun exposure than untreated skin for about 24 hours, and a laboratory study reported DNA damage in cultured keratinocytes. A 2010 EU Scientific Committee opinion found spray tanning with DHA posed no risk, though specialists criticised its reliance on industry-linked studies.[1] A fake tan does not protect against UV light.[1]
Bronzers can rub off on clothing, and tanners and bronzers can look orange or splotchy if misapplied.[1] Stretch marks and scars may take up color differently from surrounding skin, so results vary.

No studies found on sunless tanner or body makeup for hiding stretch marks or scars. Research on stretch mark treatment has generally focused on tretinoin, lasers and similar interventions, and Wikipedia's stretch marks article reports no clearly useful treatment established.[3]

Related studies of sunless tanning itself include a 2018 analysis of the 2015 US National Health Interview Survey (27,353 adults) in which 6.4% reported sunless tanning, with use associated with being young, female and non-Hispanic white,[4] and the colour-tonality and formulation studies above.[5][6]

timeline.event: Eva Wittgenstein observes DHA staining skin.[1]
Man-Tan and Coppertone QT become the first commercial DHA self-tanners.[1]
Automated spray-tan booths broaden the market.[1]

lore.intro: Sunless tanning and bronzer are discussed on looksmax.org as ways to improve face and skin colour, mostly around product choice and application.[7][8]

claims.claim: Bronzer and contour can change the look of the whole face.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread title says you can pretty much change your entire face with bronzer and contour or fake tan.[10]
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes cosmetic camouflage as covering skin imperfections and notes it may reduce their psychological impact; no trials measure facial reshaping by bronzer.[2]

claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread argues darker Indian users should use bronzer.[9]
claims.experts: No published studies have examined this claim.

claims.claim: Patchy self-tanner can be fixed by exfoliating.
claims.believers: A reply in a looksmax.org thread recommends scrubbing with an abrasive such as salt or sugar mixed with oil to remove uneven tan.[7]
claims.experts: DHA colour sits in the dead outer skin layer and fades as cells shed over about 3 to 10 days.[1]

chain: Tanner or makeup adds colour to the skin surface
Contrast between marks and surrounding skin is reduced
Skin looks more even and bronzed for days (tanner) or hours (makeup)
angle.text: Tanner and body makeup change how skin colour reads, so a stretch mark, scar or pale patch stands out less against tanned or evenly coloured skin. The result is temporary and cosmetic; texture is unchanged.
